You should try installing it in VirtualBox first. It is free Virtual Machine software, you can just install and run linux in a window on your current machine. This will allow you to learn without potentially destroying the working boot process or OS you have now. People will say "nah just install it and dual boot", but if something goes wrong it can ruin your entire week.
Not to mention that this way you can always try a few different flavors of linux as well
As for rolling distros I suggest Manjaro. If you like lightweight go with xfce, if you want more bells and whistles go with kde

An experiment in a VPN is one thing but just be wary of suggestions of what distro to go with for your final install. Rolling distros are much more bleeding edge and capable of breaking than distros like Mint/Ubuntu that update every 6months or two years for the LTS versions. If you rely on this for work I would go with the latter option but Manjaro is reasonably friend if you decide you like the rolling option. You can already see a tongue in cheek post below saying to install gentoo and some of the other harder distros for beginners. You'll find some good reading on "Rolling vs Standard release" if you do a search on it.

I've been running Arch Linux for a year now and only one time, I had to delete some old packages manually for updates to work again. Manjaro makes extra sure that stuff works. The risk of using a rolling release distro is non-existant, as far as I can tell, and the benefits of getting faster security + software updates are totally worth the slight occasional inconvenience.

The only thing I've heard about (not sure if it's true) is that if you update too rarely, the large jumps can cause issues. Just make sure to sudo pacman -Syu frequently.

If you only update a few times a year, then go with debian or something. Otherwise Manjaro/Arch is great. I would also recommend the latter for easy access to the Arch User Repository.
